In mathematics, '''rational reconstruction''' is a method that allows one to recover a [[rational number]] from its value [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] a [[sufficiently large]] [[integer]].

==Problem statement==
In the rational reconstruction problem, one is given as input a value <math>n \equiv r/s\pmod{m}</math>. That is,
<math>n</math> is an integer with the property that <math>ns\equiv r\pmod{m}</math>. The rational number <math>r/s</math> is unknown,
and the goal of the problem is to recover it from the given information.

In order for the problem to be solvable, it is necessary to assume that the modulus <math>m</math> is sufficiently large relative to <math>r</math> and <math>s</math>.
Typically, it is assumed that a range for the possible values of <math>r</math> and <math>s</math> is known: <math>|r| < N</math> and <math>0 < s < D</math> for some two
numerical parameters <math>N</math> and <math>D</math>. Whenever <math>m > 2ND</math> and a solution exists, the solution is unique and can be found efficiently.

==Solution==
Using a method from [[Paul S. Wang]], it is possible to recover <math>r/s</math> from <math>n</math> and <math>m</math> using the [[Euclidean algorithm]], as follows.<ref>{{citation|last=Wang|first=Paul S.|contribution=A p-adic algorithm for univariate partial fractions|doi=10.1145/800206.806398|isbn=0-89791-047-8|location=New York, NY, USA|pages=212–217|publisher=Association for Computing Machinery|title=Proceedings of the Fourth International Symposium on Symbolic and Algebraic Computation (SYMSAC '81)|year=1981|title-link=International Symposium on Symbolic and Algebraic Computation|s2cid=10695567 }}</ref><ref>{{citation|last1=Wang|first1=Paul S.|last2=Guy|first2=M. J. T.|author2-link=Michael Guy|last3=Davenport|first3=J. H.|author3-link=James H. Davenport|date=May 1982|doi=10.1145/1089292.1089293|issue=2|journal=ACM SIGSAM Bulletin|location=New York, NY, USA|pages=2–3|publisher=Association for Computing Machinery|title=P-adic reconstruction of rational numbers|volume=16|citeseerx=10.1.1.395.6529|s2cid=44536107 }}.</ref>

One puts <math>v = (m,0)</math> and <math>w = (n,1)</math>. One then repeats the following steps until the first component of ''w'' becomes <math>\leq N</math>. Put <math>q = \left\lfloor{\frac{v_{1}}{w_{1}}}\right\rfloor</math>, put ''z'' = ''v''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''qw''. The new ''v'' and ''w'' are then obtained by putting ''v'' = ''w'' and ''w'' = ''z''.

Then with ''w'' such that <math>w_{1}\leq N</math>, one makes the second component positive by putting ''w'' = &minus;''w'' if <math>w_{2}<0</math>. If <math>w_2<D</math> and <math>\gcd(w_1,w_2)=1</math>, then the fraction <math>\frac{r}{s}</math> exists and <math>r = w_{1}</math> and <math>s = w_{2}</math>, else no such fraction exists.
